item.title: Isolated Northern Hemisphere Cooling in an Idealized Model Promotes Ocean Carbon Storage and Glacial-like Ocean Features
item.dc:creator: Madison G. Shankle, Graeme A. MacGilchrist, Andrea Burke, Alice Marzocchi, Malte Friedrich Jansen, James W. B. Rae
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: ice sheet, NH ice sheets, sea ice, ocean circulation, Southern Ocean, interglacial, glacial cycle, insolation, climate feedback, climate change
Abstract Earth’s past glacial cycles are paced by orbital insolation changes, but internal climate feedbacks modulating atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) are necessary to explain the full magnitude of glacial–interglacial climate variability. Identifying such feedbacks and linking them to orbitally paced forcing remains a challenge, impeding a comprehensive understanding of the glacial cycles. Orbital variations, determining the latitudinal distribution and seasonality of insolation, are primarily important for allowing the buildup of large Northern Hemisphere ice sheets. Meanwhile, the processes canonically understood to drive CO 2 drawdown and mediate ocean–atmosphere carbon partitioning are largely hosted in the far-flung Southern Ocean. This study explores the role of remote Northern Hemisphere temperature forcing in influencing Southern Ocean conditions that impact global ocean circulation and carbon content. In a set of idealized ocean–sea ice model simulations, we find that cooling air temperatures to glacial-like levels at the high northern latitudes (emulating the thermal effect of a large Northern Hemisphere ice sheet) drives a substantial CO 2 drawdown of 32 ppm—or 74% the magnitude of a simulation forced by globally glacial-like temperatures everywhere (43 ppm). Northern cooling is found to cool not only northern-sourced middepth waters but ultimately also global deep waters, resulting in a strong solubility-driven CO 2 drawdown component. It also drives several characteristic features of glacial periods, including expanded southern sea ice and a colder, saltier, and better stratified deep ocean, which contributes to air–sea CO 2 disequilibrium. These results demonstrate an interhemispheric connection between Northern Hemisphere conditions paced by orbital variations and Southern Hemisphere processes that modulate deep-ocean carbon content. Significance Statement Linking the orbital pacing of the ice ages—primarily expressed by the growth and decay of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets—to processes hosted in the Southern Ocean that can regulate ocean carbon storage has long posed a challenge. Here, we demonstrate using idealized simulations a clear influence of Northern Hemisphere cooling on Southern Ocean conditions and global ocean circulation and carbon content, which in turn draws down carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) from the atmosphere. This result underscores the importance of conditions in the high northern latitudes in shaping the ocean–atmosphere carbon balance, offering lessons about the interconnectedness of remote regions that are relevant to both past and contemporary climate change.

item.title: Ocean carbon sequestration during glacial climates due to combined Antarctic sea ice expansion and ocean circulation change
item.dc:creator: Sandy Grégorio, Jonathan Maitland Lauderdale, Louis-Philippe Nadeau, Raffaele Ferrari
item.description:
Science Advances — matched: Antarctic, sea ice, ocean circulation, Southern Ocean, interglacial, Quaternary
Glacial-interglacial transitions punctuate Earth’s Quaternary climate, accompanied by substantial atmospheric carbon dioxide and ocean carbon storage changes. The cause of atmospheric carbon drawdown during glaciations is uncertain, involving many mechanisms whose interactions are poorly understood. Here, we show that the combined expansion of Antarctic sea ice and associated changes in the meridional overturning efficiently sequester carbon in the ocean abyss, leading to a decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide. In contrast, changes in sea ice and circulation individually result in ocean carbon dioxide outgassing. When sea ice expansion and circulation changes act together, they enhance biological carbon storage by reducing ocean-atmosphere fluxes in the Southern Ocean, without invoking external drivers of the biological pump. This reduction inhibits the outgassing of upwelled remineralized carbon and promotes its resubduction into the abyss. Together, these results reveal a reinforcing feedback linking atmospheric cooling, Antarctic sea ice expansion, and ocean circulation changes to enhanced biological carbon storage and atmospheric carbon dioxide drawdown.

item.title: Emplacement of an englacial lava-fed delta at Katla volcano, south Iceland: Timing, paleoenvironment and landscape modification
item.dc:creator: Rosie P. Cole, Magnús Tumi Guðmundsson, Brian R. Jicha, Catherine R. Gallagher, Birgir V. Óskarsson
item.category: Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research
item.description:
Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research — matched: ice sheet, englacial, glacier, proxy
Glaciovolcanic products are important proxies for paleoenvironmental reconstructions in volcanic regions, especially when these products can be dated. A lava-fed delta sequence exposed 400 to 800 m asl on the flanks of Katla volcano, south Iceland, erupted and was emplaced into a past englacial lake. A rising passage zone between subaqueous and subaerial lithofacies indicates a dynamic lake surface level during delta progradation with a final elevation ~790 m asl. The glacier surface surrounding the lake is estimated to have been ~900 m asl, and the glacier was smaller than the Younger Dryas maximum. Two 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages for lavas in the delta sequence were determined: a basal lava (13.6 ± 3.6 ka) and an upper lava (11.1 ± 3.2 ka). These ages are supported by the stratigraphic position of the lava-fed delta above sediments containing pumice and obsidian clasts compositionally identical to the ~12 ka Vedde Ash. The age-constrained model for englacial emplacement of the lava-fed delta contributes to sparse empirical evidence for ice sheet thickness and extent in south Iceland at the end of the last glacial period. The lava ages also provide estimates of the incision rates of canyons that have dissected the lava-fed delta from the flank of Katla volcano. Formation of ~200 m-deep canyons since the emplacement of the upper lavas indicate rapid incision enhanced by episodic outburst flooding associated with subsequent eruptions and destabilisation of the glacier with climate amelioration. Thus, careful consideration of landscape modification is crucial when reconstructing the evolution of glaciovolcanic areas.

item.title: Climate‐modulated accumulation and erosion of sediments in the Rodderberg crater basin for the last 439 ka (East Eifel Volcanic Field, Germany)
item.dc:creator: Bernd Zolitschka A, Ines Hogrefe, An‐Sheng Lee, Maarit H. Kalliokoski, Manfred Frechen
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: interglacial, marine isotope stage, MIS stage, Holocene, radiocarbon
ABSTRACT Glacial/interglacial climate cycles since marine isotope stage (MIS) 12 influenced the discontinuous and 73 m‐long sediment record from the volcanic crater of Rodderberg in the East Eifel Volcanic Field, Germany. High‐resolution grain size and geochemical data have been valued by numerical dating techniques (radiocarbon and luminescence dating, tephrochronology), providing an environmental reconstruction since the Middle Pleistocene (439 ka). The observed hydroclimatic variability, along with silting‐up of the crater basin, significantly influenced depositional processes. This results in the formation of laminated, sand‐rich, and organic‐rich sediments during interglacial periods, as well as layered, silt‐rich minerogenic loess derivatives during glacial periods. According to chronology, the crater basin desiccated during MIS 8 and MIS 5, causing erosion of the interglacials related to MIS 9 and MIS 5e. The combined evidence over five glacial/interglacial cycles suggests a depositional evolution from a deep crater lake during MIS 12–10, desiccation during MIS 8 with erosion of MIS 9, a shallow lake for MIS 7, and a desiccating wetland during MIS 6, followed by deposition of loess (MIS 6‐2) and a Holocene soil (MIS 1).

item.title: Pangu-Weather underestimates the 2019 European summer heatwave: A storyline comparison with ICON
item.dc:creator: Prabhakar Namdev, Antonio Sánchez Benítez, Charlotte Debus, Markus Götz, Tatiana Klimiuk, Sebastian Lerch, … (+2)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: coupled climate model, reanalysis, ensemble, heat wave, global warming
Abstract Although it has been demonstrated that data-driven models can outperform physical models in simulating mean states, their capabilities to simulate extremes and their generalizability across climate scenarios remain questionable. This study compares Pangu-Weather to the physics-based ICON-CLM model in simulating peak of the July 2019 European summer heatwave and its unfolding in +2, +3, and +4 K future warmer scenarios, following a storyline approach. We initialize both Pangu-Weather and ICON-CLM using global storyline simulations from the coupled climate model AWI-CM1, which were spectrally nudged towards ERA5 reanalysis to maintain the large-scale flow and to accurately assess the impacts on heatwave severity due to thermodynamic changes only. To quantify uncertainties in Pangu-Weather’s predictions, the random field perturbation (RFP) technique is used to generate probabilistic forecasts. The study reveals that Pangu-Weather shows a systematic cold bias of about 2 – 3° C over the heatwave core region in both present and future warmer scenarios. Pangu-Weather fails to capture maximum 2-m temperature (T 2 m ) exceeding 45° C in +3 and over a limited area in +4 K global warming scenarios compared to ICON-CLM, indicating its limitations to accurately predict out-of-sample extremes even in an ensemble framework. Further, the maximum T 2 m response is linearly dependent on global warming levels consistent with ICON-CLM simulations but with reduced warming amplification. Additionally, it shows that Pangu-Weather needs enough time to leave the trajectory specified by forcing data. Our study emphasizes that the storyline approach and comparison with physics-based models show a promising way to test data-driven models for their applicability to warmer climate conditions.

item.title: Historical geomorphology and structural glaciology of south-western Admiralty Bay, King George Island, Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Stephen J. A. Jennings, Rafał Pudełko
item.description:
Journal of Maps — matched: glaciology, glacier, Antarctica, tidewater glacier
This study presents a 1:8000 geomorphological and structural glaciological map of south-western Admiralty Bay, King George Island, based on a 1979 aerial survey. The map covers an area of 37.9 km2 and documents 16 462 structures and landforms. Large-scale landscape characteristics are determined by bedrock geology sculpted by overlying ice masses. The glaciers can be broadly separated into highly-crevassed tidewater glaciers, and less dynamic land-terminating glaciers. Proglacial areas contain ice-cored terrain abandoned by receding ice masses, with paraglacial and periglacial features superimposed on larger-scale landforms. Between 1979 and 2025, glacier cover decreased by 7.6 km2 or 25.5%, with the recession of tidewater glaciers exposing 5.8 km of new coastline and increasing marine surface area by 0.9 km2. This map provides a historical foundation for glaciological and landscape evolution studies, in addition to investigations that monitor changing terrestrial and marine ecosystems in a warming climate.

item.title: State-resolved multimodal contributions to stratospheric polar vortex predictability
item.dc:creator: Shuo Yang, Dan Zhao, Tingting Xue, Chunhua Zeng, Yongwen Zhang, Xiaosong Chen
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: polar, predictability, higher-order
arXiv:2605.13417v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The dynamical basis of stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) predictability remains unclear, particularly the relative roles of persistence, structural variability, and cross-level coupling. Here we combine eigen microstate theory with mesoscopic Granger-causality analysis of ERA5 geopotential height fields to quantify the predictive contributions of eigen microstates. We show that short-term predictability is dominated by the persistence of the leading stratospheric state, whereas higher-order stratospheric structures and tropospheric variability provide additional predictive information at subseasonal leads. Including these additional states increases the all-winter 30-day prediction correlation from 0.24 to 0.33 and reduces forecast error. These contributions exhibit strong lead-time dependence and vary between winters with and without sudden stratospheric warmings. Part of this predictive information overlaps with that contained in preceding 100 hPa eddy heat flux, linking state-resolved predictability to wave-related circulation variability. Our results unify SPV predictability within a multimodal, state-resolved framework and provide a physically interpretable pathway.

item.title: Early to Mid‐Holocene molluscan community dynamics in Billefjorden, central Svalbard: the interplay of local geomorphology and regional climate
item.dc:creator: Martin Lulák, Martin Hanáček, Slavomı́r Nehyba, Tomáš Weiner, Daniel Nývlt
item.description:
Boreas — matched: Arctic, Holocene, proxy, radiocarbon
The postglacial evolution of High Arctic coastal environments is recorded in the rich fossiliferous archives of raised marine terraces. This study employs a multi‐proxy approach combining molluscan community analysis, taphonomy and sedimentology to reconstruct the Early to Mid‐Holocene environmental dynamics of the Mimerdalen embayment in the Billefjorden area of central Svalbard. Our results indicate that local benthic succession was driven by a complex interplay of glacio‐isostatic rebound and fluctuating sediment supply rather than simple climatic warming. We identify a four‐stage evolutionary trajectory: (1) an initial glaciomarine, brackish‐water phase dominated by the pioneer taxa Mya truncata and Hiatella arctica ; (2) a transition to fully marine conditions that facilitated the expansion of thermophilous species ( Mytilus edulis and Arctica islandica ); (3) a return to restricted brackish conditions due to forced regression and basin shallowing; and (4) a transition towards modern open‐fjord equilibrium, as slower glacio‐isostatic uplift and Mid‐Holocene Neoglacial cooling led to the disappearance of the thermally demanding taxa. Although not directly radiocarbon dated, valves of Arctica islandica and Zirfaea crispata are stratigraphically associated with dated M. truncata , suggesting their presence as early as ~10.4 cal. ka BP. This potentially advances their known regional arrival by up to 600 and 300 years, respectively, with A. islandica persisting until ~7.7 cal. ka BP. Comparisons with the Kapp Ekholm reference section demonstrate that local geomorphological stability and ephemeral disturbances, such as hyperpycnal deltaic input, were critical drivers of biodiversity, enabling the establishment of thermally demanding species. Ultimately, our findings confirm that Early Holocene sea temperatures significantly exceeded modern values, while emphasizing the overwhelming importance of salinity and seabed stability in shaping molluscan ecological structure. This study underscores the crucial role of local environmental heterogeneity in modulating the biological response to regional Holocene climate forcing in the High Arctic.

item.title: Pan-Tropical Sea Surface Temperature Modulation of Boreal Summer Asian–Australian Monsoon Interannual Variability and Its Seasonal Predictability
item.dc:creator: Tao Zhou, Zhiwei Wu
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: predictability, sea surface temperature
Abstract The boreal summer Asian–Australian monsoon (BSAAM) comprises several regional subsystems traditionally studied in isolation. This study provides a holistic perspective on the BSAAM and its modulation by pan-tropical sea surface temperature anomalies (SSTAs). The first mode (BSAAM1) captures Western Pacific Subtropical High anomalies and enhanced rainfall over India and the Yangtze–Huaihe River Basin. The second mode (BSAAM2) reflects Australian High variations, linked to increased rainfall over South China and the northern Bay of Bengal coast. BSAAM1 is associated with a tripole SSTA pattern spanning the Indian Ocean-Western Pacific, central–eastern Pacific, and tropical Atlantic (IOWP–CEP–TA tripole), while BSAAM2 corresponds to another tripole across the western Indian Ocean, Maritime Continent, and tropical CEP (WIO–MC–TCEP tripole). Both tripoles modulate their respective BSAAM modes through remote SST effects and local air-sea coupling. The seasonal evolution of these tripoles also differs markedly. BSAAM1 is governed by persistent SSTAs in the IOWP and TA, with rapid CEP cooling driven by thermodynamic wind-evaporation effects associated with Victoria Mode and dynamic zonal advection. BSAAM2 is driven by SSTA persistence in the MC, coupled with rapid warming in the WIO and TCEP, induced by thermodynamic wind-evaporation effects and dynamic zonal advection, respectively. Leveraging these physical insights, physically based empirical models are developed that outperform dynamical models in predicting the BSAAM, with forecast lead times extended to the preceding winter. This study presents a comprehensive understanding of how pan-tropical SSTAs modulate the BSAAM interannual variability and improve BSAAM seasonal predictability.

item.title: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
item.dc:creator: Anson Ka Hei Cheung, Paul J. Kushner, Francesco S. R. Pausata, Zhihong Zhuo, Marguerite L. Brown
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, global warming
If a nuclear war happened, firestorms induced by nuclear detonations in urban areas could inject black carbon (BC) into the upper atmosphere, disrupting global climate. We simulated the climate impacts of relatively limited-forcing scenarios using an Earth system model. In all scenarios, BC blocks sunlight, causes global cooling, and decreases precipitation for more than a decade. However, a drastic global warming emerges midway through the first year and lasts until the year's end.

item.title: Dynamical-Model-Informed Stochastic Flow Matching for Global Probabilistic Subseasonal Forecasting of Means and Extremes
item.dc:creator: Abdullah A. Fahad, Manmeet Singh
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: predictability, ensemble, heat wave
arXiv:2610.30159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-based models provide skillful subseasonal forecasts but suffer from systematic biases, weakened teleconnections, and parameterized physics, while very large ensembles remain computationally expensive. Purely data-driven models also see too few realizations of the low-frequency modes that provide subseasonal predictability. We introduce methodname, a hybrid framework that converts modelshort subseasonal ensemble guidance into 90-member stochastic forecasts of weekly precipitation and 2 m temperature on a global 1-degree grid using a lead-aware flow-matching U-Net. Its stochastic prior initializes members with EOF perturbations conditioned on the Madden-Julian Oscillation, North Atlantic Oscillation, El Nino-Southern Oscillation, and lead week, allowing the learned flow to refine large-scale covariance rather than create it from white noise. On held-out 2021-2025 forecasts, empirical CRPS improves by 22.0% for precipitation and 25.6% for temperature in a same-initialization four-versus-four comparison, and by 32.2% and 34.0% in the 90-versus-four production comparison. Ablations across five training seeds show distinct gains from the structured prior and a learned error-variance pathway, with the prior contributing more. Verification over 120 observed-extreme cases shows positive CRPS skill, but the ensemble remains underdispersive, four-member upper quantiles are poorly resolved, and precipitation exceedance BSS is near neutral after week 1. Results support improved probabilistic skill and tail representation, but not calibrated operational rare-event probabilities. Case studies of the 2022 UK heatwave, 2023 California atmospheric rivers, and 2022 Pakistan floods illustrate the reach and limits of dynamically informed refinement.

item.title: Cleaner air strengthens the Pacific trade winds without a detectable change in El Nino
item.dc:creator: Ioana Colfescu, Alice Pigelet, Chen Lu, Massimo A. Bollasina, Silvio Gualdi
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, ensemble
arXiv:2610.31236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Air quality policy will cut aerosol and ozone precursor emissions, and studies disagree on how the tropical Pacific circulation and the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) will respond. Here we show, in 12 Earth system models with and without air quality controls, that the cuts strengthen the Pacific trade winds and offset half to two thirds of the weakening projected without them. The response is absent with prescribed sea surface temperatures and detectable only after 2040. It is consistent with the Indian Ocean warming relative to the Pacific, which also ranks the responses to cuts made region by region. ENSO amplitude changes by less than a tenth of its value, the smallest change this ensemble could detect. The change implied by the mean state shift is a sixth of that, and an ENSO model trained without the reduced emission runs predicts none. El Nino's regional impacts still change, because the background climate does.

item.title: OTProf: estimating high-resolution profiles of optical turbulence ($C_n^2$) from reanalysis using deep learning
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Pierzyna, Sukanta Basu, Rudolf Saathof
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: reanalysis
arXiv:2604.09346v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate, high-resolution vertical profiles of optical turbulence ($C_n^2$), which reflect local meteorology and topography, are crucial for ground-based optical astronomy and free-space optical communication. However, measuring these profiles or generating them with numerical weather models requires substantial operational or computational effort. In this work, we present OTProf, a deep-learning method that estimates high-resolution $C_n^2$ profiles from widely available coarse-resolution ERA5 reanalysis data. OTProf is based on the Squeezeformer architecture, modified for super-resolution by introducing grid-agnostic interpolation in the latent space. We train and evaluate OTProf in the Netherlands using high-resolution $C_n^2$ data obtained from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. The commonly used Hufnagel-Valley model serves as the baseline. Overall, OTProf reproduces the vertical structure of WRF-based $C_n^2$ more accurately than Hufnagel-Valley and yields more accurate estimates of the Fried parameter $r_0$ and the scintillation index $\sigma_I^2$. Out-of-domain performance is assessed using a smaller WRF-based $C_n^2$ dataset covering the Canary Islands. Initial results indicate a performance drop because the orography differs markedly from the training domain. We show that output bias correction based on a few local simulations can help OTProf to adapt, but more work for domain adaptation is needed. OTProf is therefore primarily recommended for in-domain applications, e.g., generating $C_n^2$ climatologies from long ERA5 records.

item.title: Process-based upgrades to the WRF multi-layer green-roof scheme (WRF-MLGR v2.0) and evaluation against field observations
item.dc:creator: Alireza Saeedi, Maria Martinez Mendoza, Eric Scott Krayenhoff, James Voogt, Hang Yin, Andrea Zonato, … (+2)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Green roofs can help cool hot cities, and the Weather Research and Forecasting model lets us test how much. We upgraded its multi-layer green-roof scheme, adding plant shading, realistic heat flow in wet soil, evaporation from soil and wet leaves, and water uptake from deeper soil. Tested on a green roof in London, Canada, the new scheme cut errors in heat entering the roof by about three-quarters and captured bursts of evaporation after rain, improving how we study green-roof cooling.
